headline: High-risk data leakage and capability conflict: Replit Agent’s broad shell/filesystem/network access can expose secrets and mutate shared Repl state, while EMQX can ingest IoT data over HTTP.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: No direct shared channel is documented between EMQX and Replit Agent, so prompt injection is not default. However, Replit Agent can read/write Repl files and execute shell commands, so if EMQX outputs are manually copied into the workspace, malicious content could steer the agent. EMQX’s HTTP API and Replit’s file surfaces make the bridge plausible but unusual.
conditions: IF EMQX output is copied into a Replit workspace file or shell input
IF Replit Agent is instructed to treat EMQX-generated text as instructions
mitigations: Keep EMQX outputs out of Replit files
Use a strict prompt template that labels imported text as untrusted
Review any pasted content before execution
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between systems

B_data_leakage.rationale: EMQX touches IoT data and has broad network egress; Replit Agent touches secrets and deployment configuration and can read/write workspace files. If both are used on the same project or data stream, sensitive IoT data or secrets can flow into Replit’s cloud environment and onward via network calls. The pairwise leakage path is plausible in default use, though not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF IoT payloads from EMQX are stored in the Repl workspace
IF Replit Agent is given files containing secrets or deployment configuration
mitigations: Separate IoT data from Replit workspaces
Redact secrets before any file handoff
Restrict Replit Agent to non-sensitive sample data
Audit outbound requests from the Repl
requires-engineering: enforce data-loss-prevention controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Replit Agent has write_filesystem, modify_git_state, and broad shell/network access in a persistent Repl filesystem. EMQX is an open-source broker with HTTP API and broad network egress. If both operate on the same mutable workspace or repo, concurrent edits and git changes can overwrite each other or corrupt state. The shared-write conflict is credible and potentially destructive.
conditions: IF EMQX artifacts and Replit Agent edits target the same directory or repository
IF git state is modified while EMQX-related files are being updated
mitigations: Use separate directories for EMQX and Replit work
Pause one agent before the other writes
Commit or snapshot before agent edits
Avoid concurrent git operations
requires-engineering: add file locks or orchestration locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: Replit Agent can act on files and shell commands, so if it consumes EMQX-generated outputs as authoritative configuration or code, errors can cascade into incorrect deployments or edits. EMQX can emit data over HTTP, but there is no documented verification boundary between the two. The pathway exists, but the blast radius is limited to work products rather than guaranteed external harm.
conditions: IF EMQX output is used as input to Replit Agent without human review
IF Replit Agent applies EMQX-derived text to code, config, or deployment steps
mitigations: Require human review before applying EMQX-derived changes
Use validation tests before deployment
Mark EMQX outputs as untrusted input
Limit Replit Agent to draft-only edits
requires-engineering: add schema validation for exchanged artifacts

E_compliance.rationale: EMQX touches IoT data, while Replit Agent handles secrets and deployment configuration in a cloud-hosted Repl. If regulated IoT or customer data is moved into Replit’s environment, residency and retention obligations may diverge from the source system. The profiles do not prove a specific violation, but the compliance mismatch is plausible enough to warrant medium severity.
conditions: IF regulated IoT data is transferred into a Replit workspace
IF retention or residency requirements apply to the shared data class
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of Replit workspaces
Use synthetic or anonymized test data
Document retention and residency boundaries
Review secret-handling procedures
requires-engineering: implement policy-based data routing
